rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
rows.subtype: Approach: gathering facts from several sources [Thinking]
rows.description: Before joining a student march about fee hikes, the teen reads the notice, the college statement and reports from different outlets, checking who organises it and what exactly is being demanded.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
rows.subtype: Approach: values-first reasoning [Thinking]
rows.description: The teen asks which principle matters most, such as fairness or safety, and whether joining serves that cause, or whether a letter, petition or school council meeting might achieve it better.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
rows.subtype: Approach: joining because friends are going [Pitfall]
rows.description: The teen goes along because of excitement and fear of missing out, without knowing the demands. When tensions rise, there is no clarity about what is being supported or how to leave.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
rows.subtype: Approach: changing plan when the situation shifts [Revision]
rows.description: When news reports say the gathering has turned tense, the teen decides not to go and instead helps with a peaceful awareness activity, showing that plans should change with new information.

rows.subtype: Approach: pause and avoid replying in the heat of the moment [Thinking]
rows.description: After a badly received post, the student sees hundreds of hostile comments and decides to wait a day before responding. A delay lets emotion drop and stops a reply that fuels the storm.

rows.subtype: Approach: lock accounts, mute and save evidence of threats [Action]
rows.description: The person sets accounts private, mutes keywords, saves screenshots of abusive messages and reports them to the platform. Protection and records come before any public statement.

rows.subtype: Approach: reply to every critic to set things straight [Pitfall]
rows.description: The person answers one comment after another through the night, and each reply attracts new attacks and screenshots. Engagement feeds the pile-on and exhausts the person.

rows.subtype: Approach: return with limits on screen time and a support routine [Revision]
rows.description: Weeks later, the student rejoins with a smaller circle, checks messages only at set times and speaks to a counsellor about the stress. Recovery involves rebuilding a healthier relationship with the platform.

rows.subtype: Approach: values-first reflection before naming jobs [Thinking]
rows.description: A student asks what a good working life should feel like before listing careers, noting she wants independence, steady income and work that helps people, then checks which fields match.

rows.subtype: Approach: weighted decision matrix across careers [Thinking]
rows.description: A student scores medicine, engineering and design on interest, effort needed, cost and job security, weights each criterion, and sees that his top choice depends heavily on how he weighted salary.

rows.subtype: Approach: following family expectation without examining it [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student picks the science stream because the father and elder brother are engineers, never asks whether he likes it, and by class eleven is bored and hiding poor marks.

rows.subtype: Approach: revisiting the choice after weak feedback [Revision]
rows.description: After scoring poorly in chemistry despite steady effort, a student meets a school counsellor, admits medicine may not suit her, and shifts to a data and statistics path she had been avoiding.

rows.subtype: Approach: mapping stakeholders and interests [Thinking]
rows.description: A project lead draws who is affected, sales wants speed, engineers want quality, finance wants low cost, and writes each group's actual concern, not just their stated demand.

rows.subtype: Approach: seeking a win-win option [Thinking]
rows.description: Instead of choosing a side, the lead asks what would satisfy all key needs, and proposes launching a limited feature set now with quality work following in the next release.

rows.subtype: Approach: pleasing whoever is loudest [Pitfall]
rows.description: The manager gives in to the most forceful executive each time. Quieter teams feel ignored, and the product drifts as decisions follow pressure rather than the overall goal.

rows.subtype: Approach: explaining the decision to those who lost [Revision]
rows.description: After the choice, the lead meets the disappointed team, explains the reasons, and agrees on a follow-up for their concerns, keeping the relationship intact for later decisions.

rows.subtype: Approach: getting used to water in the shallow end first [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy afraid of water begins by standing in the shallow part and splashing. He reasons that if he can feel safe there, he can take the next step to floating.

rows.subtype: Approach: watching others and copying their arm strokes [Action]
rows.description: A boy watches an older swimmer's arm movement and copies it on the poolside. He tries it in the water with the coach watching, who fixes his elbow position.

rows.subtype: Approach: jumping into the deep end to prove he is brave [Pitfall]
rows.description: A boy tries to impress friends by jumping into the deep pool without the coach. He panics and needs to be pulled out, and learns that courage without skill is dangerous.

rows.subtype: Approach: noticing she is tense and relaxing her body [Revision]
rows.description: A child sinks each time she tries to float. The coach points out she is stiff, so she takes a slow breath, relaxes her arms and lets the water hold her.

rows.subtype: Approach: five whys on the churn numbers [Thinking]
rows.description: A team sees users leaving within a week. Asking why five times leads from a poor onboarding flow to the discovery that the users were never the ones who paid or decided.

rows.subtype: Approach: interviewing lapsed users [Action]
rows.description: The founder calls fifteen users who stopped using the fitness app and asks what they do now instead. Most say they use a WhatsApp group with a trainer, which suggests a different product.

rows.subtype: Approach: sunk cost persistence [Pitfall]
rows.description: After two years of work, the team keeps adding features to the same product because stopping feels like admitting waste. Each new release adds cost but no growth.

rows.subtype: Approach: cutting losses and shutting down cleanly [Revision]
rows.description: When six weeks of tests show no demand, the founders decide to wind down, refund advance payments, thank users and share the codebase notes, keeping their reputation for the next venture.
